messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 67
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: School Principal
  trauma_type: Life-threatening motor vehicle collision
  pcl5: 48

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Shouting: Shouting, Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident, Auditory (Loud Noises): Loud noises
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Work or Study: Going to work or study, Positive Reframing: I force myself to think only positive thoughts, Overeat: eat excessively to manage distress
  Threat: Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening, Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep, Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place
  Memory: Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words., Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over., Reliving Event: When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now.
  Negative Appraisals: Self-Comparison: Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation, Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Clinical Vignette: Martin K.

Three years ago, Martin K. was driving home from a school board meeting on a Tuesday evening when a pickup truck ran a red light and collided with the driver's side of his sedan. The impact came without warning—a shattering explosion of metal and glass, the sensation of being hurled sideways, the smell of burnt rubber and antifreeze. Martin's left arm broke in two places. He lost consciousness briefly and woke to the sound of sirens, unable at first to understand where he was or whether he was dying. The other driver walked away with minor injuries. Martin spent two nights in hospital and six weeks in a sling.

He returned to work after the medical leave, determined to resume his life. But something had fractured in him that the X-rays had not captured. Within weeks, he noticed that loud noises—a car backfiring, a door slamming in the hallway, the screech of bus brakes in the school parking lot—sent a jolt of pure panic through his chest. His heart would race. His hands would shake. He had come to believe that these sounds were warnings, harbingers of the collision happening again. When he heard shouting—a teacher raising her voice to a student, an angry parent on the phone—Martin's entire body tensed. The sound seemed to contain the same violence as the impact itself, and he found himself unable to stay in the room.

The memories themselves had taken on a quality that terrified him. He could not quite put the event into words when he tried to describe it to his wife, Patricia. Instead, the crash played in his mind like a film looping endlessly—the moment before impact, the shattering, the disorientation, again and again. When these memories arrived, particularly in the dark of night, Martin did not feel as though he were remembering something that had happened; he felt as though it were happening now, in real time, his body responding with the full force of terror. He would lie awake, rigid, waiting for sleep that would not come. Even on nights when exhaustion finally pulled him under, he would wake gasping, drenched in sweat, his mind unable to distinguish between the memory and present danger.

His interpretation of the world had shifted in ways he could not quite explain to others. When Patricia was late coming home from her book club, Martin did not think simply that traffic had delayed her; he became certain that something terrible had occurred, that she had been in an accident. When a staff meeting ran twenty minutes longer than scheduled, he interpreted the delay as a sign that catastrophe was unfolding somewhere. He had come to believe that the world was fundamentally dangerous, that the safety he had taken for granted before the collision had been an illusion. And he had come to believe something darker still: that he was the kind of person who should have seen the truck coming, who should have been more alert, more careful. Someone else would not have gotten into this situation. He was changed now, permanently. He was not the man he had been.

To manage the mounting distress, Martin had developed habits. He began avoiding the drive to school, asking Patricia to drop him off and pick him up, which created tension in their marriage and consumed her schedule. He forced himself to think only positive thoughts—a deliberate, exhausting effort to suppress any acknowledgment of risk. And he had begun eating more, much more, using food as a way to soothe the anxiety that never quite released its grip. His weight had increased by thirty pounds. He could not relax even in his own home, in spaces he knew were safe; his vigilance remained constant, his body perpetually braced.

Six months ago, the superintendent suggested that Martin consider stepping down from his position as principal, noting that he seemed "distracted" and "not himself." The suggestion devastated him. This year, after a particularly difficult morning when a fire alarm sent him into a panic state that left him unable to function for hours, Martin finally called his doctor. He is here now, at sixty-seven, frightened that he will never be the person he was, and hoping that someone might help him understand why a moment of terrible chance has taken such permanent hold.
